name: DISC Personality Test
tagline: Understand your work style and how you communicate.
intro: The DISC model describes four behavioural styles: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness and Conscientiousness. This test shows how strongly you use each style at work and in daily life, and which one is most natural for you. Rate 100 short statements; it takes about five minutes and gives practical tips for working with others.
seoTitle: DISC Personality Test – Free work style profile
seoDescription: Find your DISC style in 5 minutes. See your scores for Dominance, Influence, Steadiness and Conscientiousness, plus tips for communication and teamwork.

dominance.name: Dominance (D)
dominance.short: How direct, decisive and results-driven you are, and how readily you take on challenges.
dominance.low: You use the Dominance style rarely. You prefer cooperation over competition, think before you act and do not need to be in charge. Colleagues experience you as calm and considerate. The pitfall is that you may avoid tough calls or let others decide things that affect you. Tip: when something matters to you, state your position clearly and early, using short, direct sentences. Practise making small decisions quickly to build confidence for bigger ones.
dominance.mid: You can be direct and decisive when needed, but you do not always need to lead or win. You take on challenges that matter to you and are willing to let others steer at other times. This flexibility makes you a versatile team member. Tip: notice in which situations you hold back when a firm stand would help, and where you push when patience would work better. Adjust your directness to what the moment needs.
dominance.high: Dominance is a strong part of your style. You are direct, decisive and focused on results. You like challenges, make quick decisions and push to move things forward. In communication you are brief and to the point. People rely on you to get things done. The pitfall is that you may come across as impatient or blunt and overlook others' input. Tip: before deciding, ask at least one person for their view. Explain the why behind your requests; it builds commitment, not just compliance.

influence.name: Influence (I)
influence.short: How outgoing, persuasive and enthusiastic you are in working with and motivating people.
influence.low: You use the Influence style rarely. You prefer facts and tasks to small talk and are cautious about showing enthusiasm. Colleagues see you as serious and focused. The pitfall is that your good ideas may not get the attention they deserve, or people may find you distant. Tip: when presenting an idea, add a short story or example that shows why it matters to people. Take a moment for personal contact at the start of meetings; it makes collaboration smoother.
influence.mid: You can be engaging and persuasive when you want to be, but you also enjoy focused, quiet work. You connect with people easily without needing constant interaction. Tip: use your social skills deliberately, for example when you need support for an idea or want to motivate a team. At the same time, notice whether you sometimes hold back enthusiasm that could inspire others.
influence.high: Influence is a strong part of your style. You are outgoing, optimistic and persuasive. You enjoy people, build networks easily and bring energy and enthusiasm to a team. In communication you are expressive, warm and story-driven. The pitfall is that you may overpromise, lose track of details or talk more than you listen. Tip: follow up conversations with a short written summary of agreements. Pair up with detail-oriented colleagues and use checklists to turn your ideas into finished results.

steadiness.name: Steadiness (S)
steadiness.short: How patient, supportive and consistent you are, and how much you value stability and cooperation.
steadiness.low: You use the Steadiness style rarely. You like change, variety and a fast pace, and routine can make you restless. Colleagues see you as dynamic and flexible. The pitfall is that you may move on before others are ready or underestimate the value of stability. Tip: when introducing changes, give people time to adjust and explain what stays the same. Check in with quieter colleagues; their support is easier to keep than to win back.
steadiness.mid: You value stability and good relationships, but you can also handle change and a faster pace when needed. You are supportive without losing sight of your own goals. This makes you a reliable and adaptable team member. Tip: notice whether you sometimes keep quiet to avoid disrupting harmony. Sharing concerns early, in a calm way, helps the team and protects your own energy.
steadiness.high: Steadiness is a strong part of your style. You are patient, loyal and supportive, and you create a calm, cooperative atmosphere. You listen well, work consistently and prefer stable routines. People trust you and feel at ease with you. The pitfall is that sudden change can unsettle you and you may avoid conflict or saying no. Tip: ask for advance notice of changes and break them into small steps. Practise stating your view in meetings; your calm perspective is valuable.

conscientiousness.name: Conscientiousness (C)
conscientiousness.short: How careful, analytical and quality-focused you are, and how much you value accuracy and standards.
conscientiousness.low: You use the Conscientiousness style rarely. You prefer quick action and big-picture thinking to detailed analysis, and rules can feel restrictive. Colleagues see you as flexible and pragmatic. The pitfall is that errors may slip through or important details get missed. Tip: build a simple quality check into your work, such as rereading key emails or using a short checklist. Ask a detail-oriented colleague to review important documents before they go out.
conscientiousness.mid: You care about accuracy and quality where it counts, but you do not get lost in details. You can follow procedures and also improvise when needed. This balance makes you both careful and practical. Tip: decide in advance which tasks deserve extra precision, such as contracts or numbers, and which can be done quickly. That keeps your standards high without slowing you down.
conscientiousness.high: Conscientiousness is a strong part of your style. You are careful, analytical and committed to quality. You value accuracy, clear procedures and well-founded decisions, and you communicate in a precise, factual way. People trust your expertise and thoroughness. The pitfall is perfectionism or getting stuck in analysis, and others may see you as critical or distant. Tip: agree on what is good enough before you start. When giving feedback, start with what works, then share your detailed observations.

summary: You receive a score from 0 to 100 % for each of the four DISC styles; your highest score is shown as your main style. Most people use a blend of styles and adapt to the situation. DISC describes observable behaviour and communication preferences, not ability or intelligence.
